# Cup Day, or: bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite

Dear Jonno,

You’ve messaged me about the coolroom enough times now that you’re getting a blog post. This is what happens when you move to London. You lose the right to hear things over a knock-off beer and become one of my forty readers demanding content.

Mum, if you’re reading, this one’s mostly for Jonno. You can stay, but there’s swearing.

The coolroom compressor died sometime overnight between Monday and Cup Day. Didn’t give us any warning. Just quietly retired ahead of the biggest lunch we’d had booked in ages. Honestly, decent career move.

I found it at 6.40 on Tuesday morning. Thermometer said eleven degrees.

Eleven.

You know that little pause when you see something properly fucked and your brain tries to offer you a different explanation? I stood there looking at it like maybe I’d forgotten how numbers worked. Maybe eleven was good now. Maybe refrigeration had changed since Monday.

Opened the door. No.

A hundred and forty covers booked. Set menu. Three courses. Raff away, me running it. And the coolroom had decided to become a cupboard.

You would’ve cried. I want to establish that early, because I know you’re already sitting in London thinking you’d have handled it. You’ve been gone since February. You’re soft now. You’d have looked at that thermometer and asked whether we could postpone lunch.

First call was Wally from Coldline, who couldn’t get there till Wednesday. Part coming from Sydney.

There’s something very calming about being told the thing you urgently need is in another state. Really narrows down your options. Can you fix it? No. Can the bloke who fixes it fix it? Also no. Righto. Better get on with whatever this is, then.

Phil’s contribution was, “Just make it work, mate.”

Cheers, Phil. Hadn’t considered that. I was going to put a sign on the door saying THE FRIDGE IS HOT and go to the races.

“Just make it work” is not a plan. It’s what someone says before leaving you to come up with one.

So we did the stock reckoning, which was about as enjoyable as you’d expect. Lost roughly eighteen hundred bucks, mostly dairy and the duck legs. Eighteen hundred dollars is a fairly expensive way to start a Tuesday before you’ve even had a coffee.

Everything we could keep went wherever there was room: the two undercounters, the bar fridge, and half of Marta’s walk-in next door.

Marta saved our arses. I cannot stress this enough. Letting another kitchen suddenly occupy half your coolroom on Cup Day is a serious act of kindness, even if she has since made it clear that kindness is payable in croissant credit.

I owe her about three weeks of staff meal. Fair enough. At this point, if she wants lunch brought over on a little silver tray, she can have it.

The relocation involved me and Benny taking thirty kilos of beef shin down the laneway on a milk crate trolley. In the rain.

You remember the sort of trolley I mean. Something that technically has wheels but shouldn’t be trusted with anything heavier than an empty box.

One wheel fell off.

Of course it did. We were already moving beef through a wet laneway before breakfast. A functioning trolley would’ve made the whole thing suspiciously easy.

There’s a particular look two blokes give each other when a wheel falls off under thirty kilos of beef. Neither of you wants to be the first to speak because whoever speaks is probably going to have to suggest what happens next.

Anyway, we got it there. I’m telling you this now because later, during lunch, a woman on table nine asked whether the beef was “free range from the laneway”.

She’d seen us out the window.

Fair play to her. Can’t even get offended. That’s a good line, and I was annoyed I hadn’t thought of it myself.

Meanwhile, Kev went to the servo and came back with fourteen bags of ice for the old esky. Fourteen. Servo bloke asked if we were having a party.

Imagine Kev having to answer that while buying enough ice to keep a small wedding drinking for six hours. No, mate, just lunch. Very exclusive event. Everyone attending has to do a job and nobody’s enjoying the lead-up.

By then the kitchen was operating across so many fridges that getting one thing sometimes meant remembering which building it lived in.

You would’ve hated it. You used to get shitty if someone moved your tongs six inches. We had ingredients with a commute.

And before you start telling me about how hard you’re working over there, I know London has kitchens. I’m sure yours is very stressful. But I also reckon you’ve started saying “quite nice” about things and owning a coat you’re not allowed to put in the washing machine. You’re not built for laneway beef anymore.

At 12.15 we had to eighty-six the panna cotta.

That was a nice little addition to proceedings. Nothing improves a three-course set menu like suddenly losing one of the courses you’ve actually planned.

Dessert became “affogato with whatever”.

Not the official wording, presumably. But that was the brief.

And people loved it. More than the panna cotta, apparently.

I’m trying not to take that personally on behalf of every panna cotta I’ve ever made. All the weighing and setting and checking the wobble, and it turns out people are perfectly happy if you give them coffee, ice cream and whatever else has survived the morning.

There’s a lesson in that, but I don’t want to learn it.

The really annoying part, after all this, is that it was probably the best service we did all year.

Genuinely.

Everyone was locked in. Benny, Kev, everyone. There wasn’t time for the usual little bits of kitchen bullshit. You needed something, someone got it. Someone was in the weeds, someone else stepped across. Nobody needed a speech about pulling together. We had a hundred and forty lunches to get out and approximately half our refrigeration was either next door or full of servo ice.

So we got them out.

I’m not going to turn this into some beautiful thing about adversity. I’d have preferred a working coolroom. Would’ve happily had an ordinary service with the dairy still alive and all the trolley wheels attached.

But it was a very good lunch.

Even table nine seemed pleased with her locally travelled beef.

Then, because apparently the day still had one joke left, my horse in the sweep was called Ice Cold Lad.

Came second last.

You couldn’t write that without someone telling you it was a bit much.

So that’s what happened with the coolroom. Eighteen hundred bucks gone, fourteen bags of ice, one trolley wheel down, panna cotta off, Marta now entitled to a significant portion of my future cooking. A hundred and forty people fed.

Bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite. I’ve said it before, but I feel we’ve now done enough practical research to stand by it.

You’d have lost your mind. Would’ve been good to have you there.

Come home ya flog.
